# Implementation-defined behavior: Windows x86-64

This page records the implementation-defined choices currently exposed by the
supported Windows x86-64 build. It does not claim Annex F/G/H, Annex K, or
decimal floating-point conformance. WG14 N3220 is used as the C23 text
baseline. N3221's editor report states the final C23 DIS draft N3219 and N3220
have no technical-content differences; N3220's noted change is an Annex K
footnote edit. See [N3220](https://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg14/www/docs/n3220.pdf)
and [N3221](https://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg14/www/docs/n3221.htm).

## Error numbers (N3220 7.5)

The required error macros have these values: `EDOM` is 33, `ERANGE` is 34,
and `EILSEQ` is 84. `errno` is thread-local. The header also exposes POSIX-style
error names with fixed project values as extensions; those are not required C23
error macros.

## Locales (N3220 7.11)

The supported explicit locale names are `"C"`, `"POSIX"`, `"C.UTF-8"`, and
`"C.utf8"`; the two UTF-8 spellings are case-insensitive and `setlocale`
returns the canonical name `"C.UTF-8"`. No other installed locale data is
provided.

With `setlocale(category, "")`, the implementation checks `LC_ALL`, then the
category environment variable, then `LANG`; if none is set it selects UTF-8.
Environment values use the same exact supported-name policy as `setlocale`:
`C`, `POSIX`, `C.UTF-8`, and `C.utf8` are accepted (with UTF-8 aliases matched
case-insensitively). Names such as `en_US.UTF-8` are rejected; the implementation
does not parse arbitrary locale names by their codeset token. An unsupported
environment value makes the request fail without changing the locale.

All categories can be set independently, but only `LC_CTYPE` changes character
encoding and Unicode classification. In the C locale, each input byte maps to
the same-valued wide character and `MB_CUR_MAX` is 1. In the UTF-8 locale,
multibyte conversion uses UTF-8 and `MB_CUR_MAX` is 4. Numeric formatting uses
`.` as the decimal point in both states; there is no localized thousands
grouping, currency, collation, or time-name data. `localeconv()` reports the C
locale values in either state.

## Signals (N3220 7.14)

The supported signal numbers are `SIGINT` (2), `SIGILL` (4), `SIGABRT` (6),
`SIGFPE` (8), `SIGSEGV` (11), and `SIGTERM` (15). `SIGABRT` is generated by
the library; the Windows PAL provides host delivery for the other listed
signals. `raise()` on an unsupported number returns nonzero and sets `errno`
to `EINVAL`.

Handlers remain installed after delivery. The default action calls `abort()`
for `SIGABRT`, `SIGILL`, `SIGFPE`, and `SIGSEGV`; it exits with status
`128 + signal_number` for `SIGINT` and `SIGTERM`. If the PAL cannot enable host
delivery for a requested handler, `signal()` returns `SIG_ERR` and sets
`errno` from the PAL error.

N3220 7.14.1.1p3 makes returning from a handler for a computationally generated
`SIGILL`/`SIGFPE`/`SIGSEGV` undefined; p4 does not permit calling `raise()` from
a handler entered for a signal generated by `raise()`. Those cases are not
promised as ordinary handler-return or recursive-delivery behavior by this
library.

## Allocation (N3220 7.24)

`memalignment(NULL)` returns zero. For a non-null pointer it returns the
largest power of two that divides the pointer value, so an interior pointer
can have a smaller result than its allocation base. `aligned_alloc` accepts
nonzero power-of-two alignments; other alignments fail with a null result and
`EINVAL`. Allocation-size arithmetic overflow fails with `ENOMEM`.

For calls meeting the standard preconditions, `free_sized` and
`free_aligned_sized` release the block through ordinary `free`; the size and
alignment hints do not select a distinct deallocation path. This says nothing
about calls with an incorrect size or alignment, for which the standard does
not define behavior.

## Time and clocks (N3220 7.29)

`time_t` and `clock_t` are signed `long long`; `CLOCKS_PER_SEC` is 1,000,000.
`timespec_get` and `timespec_getres` support `TIME_UTC`, `TIME_MONOTONIC`,
`TIME_ACTIVE` (process CPU time), and `TIME_THREAD_ACTIVE` (calling-thread CPU
time). Realtime and CPU clocks use Windows 100 ns units; the monotonic clock
uses the Windows performance counter. `clock()` reports process CPU time in
`CLOCKS_PER_SEC` units.

Local time rules come from the Windows time-zone configuration. If the Windows
year-rule lookup fails, the PAL falls back to UTC. For years before 1601 or
after 30827, the PAL uses the nearest supported boundary year for its rule
lookup. `tm_zone` abbreviations are `"UTC"` at zero offset and numeric signed
offsets otherwise; `%z` formats the offset as `±hhmm` without a colon.

`mktime` uses the prior offset to normalize a nonexistent local time forward
through a DST gap. In a repeated hour, `tm_isdst == 0` selects standard time
and a positive `tm_isdst` selects daylight time when both candidates exist.
The synthetic US-style transition in `time_dst.c` pins these choices. The
actual transition rules depend on the machine's Windows time-zone database.
`timegm` and `mktime` normalize calendar fields; they return `(time_t)-1` and
set `EOVERFLOW` when the normalized year cannot fit in `tm_year`. `gmtime_r`
and `localtime_r` return null and set `EOVERFLOW` when they cannot produce a
representable broken-down year. A returned `time_t` value of -1 can also be the
valid instant one second before the epoch.

`strftime`/`wcsftime` emit a zone only when the zone metadata is known: UTC and
local-time results produced by the library retain that metadata across ordinary
`struct tm` copies. A user-constructed `struct tm` with only the nine standard
members initialized has no zone metadata in this implementation, so `%z` and
`%Z` produce no characters. The formatter checks extra zone-member object bytes
against known producer tokens and never dereferences an unrecognized value.
The process-lifetime abbreviation table retains at most 32 distinct
abbreviation/offset pairs. If it fills, later `localtime` results still carry
their numeric `tm_gmtoff`, but their zone token is unknown and `%z`/`%Z` emit
no characters; they are never mislabeled with another zone's data.

## Floating-point behavior (N3220 5.2.5.3.3, 7.12.1)

On this target `float` is binary32; `double` and `long double` are binary64.
`FLT_ROUNDS` queries the current rounding mode and maps nearest to 1,
toward-zero to 0, upward to 2, and downward to 3. If the mode cannot be
identified, it returns -1. The per-type `*_IS_IEC_60559` macros describe the
format precision and exponent range only; they do not claim Annex F support.

`math_errhandling` advertises `MATH_ERREXCEPT` and does not advertise
`MATH_ERRNO`: math routines report required domain, pole, and overflow
conditions through floating-point exceptions, and do not promise to set
`errno`. N3220 5.2.5.3.3 permits implementation-defined accuracy choices for
mathematical functions, and 7.12.1 leaves underflow exception reporting
implementation-defined. This project does not publish a universal ULP
bound for each function. Existing reference vectors state their own tolerances
and do not establish such a bound.

For an underflowing result, these functions return the value produced by
their implementation in the destination format: a subnormal value, a signed
zero, or, where rounding reaches the boundary, a minimum normal value. The
current rounding mode and the operations in the named function determine the
result. `FE_UNDERFLOW` is the sticky flag raised by those floating-point
operations or by an explicit `feraiseexcept` in that function; merely
returning a subnormal value does not independently set the flag. In
particular:

- `nextafter`, `nextafterf`, and `nextafterl` explicitly raise both
  `FE_UNDERFLOW` and `FE_INEXACT` when distinct arguments produce a subnormal
  or zero result.
- `fma` and `fmaf` explicitly raise `FE_UNDERFLOW` for an inexact result
  whose rounded significand is subnormal; an exact subnormal result does not
  set it through that path.
- `log1p(DBL_TRUE_MIN)` returns its input through the small-argument path;
  that path evaluates `1.0 + x` and does not itself raise `FE_UNDERFLOW`.
- `remainder` can return an exact subnormal without raising `FE_UNDERFLOW`;
  its integer-quotient reduction uses exact scaling and subtraction for that
  case.

For other inputs, the operations and explicit exception raises in the
corresponding `src/math` function define the result and sticky flags. This
describes the implementation's operation-level policy rather than a claim
that all functions use one rounding algorithm.

No optional IEC feature-test macro is advertised by the production build.
